claim: C. elegans has 302 neurons that are named and have stereotyped locations across animals.
source: The nervous system of the nematode C. elegans is well characterized, such that each of the 302 neurons is named and has stereotyped locations across animals (White et al., 1986; Sulston, 1976; Witvliet et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to White et al., 1986; Sulston, 1976; Witvliet et al., 2020

claim: The variability in neurons' spatial arrangement in C. elegans is sufficient to make predicting neural correspondence a challenge.
source: Despite the worm's overall stereotypy, the variability in neurons' spatial arrangement is sufficient to make predicting neural correspondence a challenge.
evidence: Based on the authors' assessment of the problem domain

claim: Nuclear localized markers used in whole-brain calcium imaging obscure morphological features that would assist in neural identification.
source: For whole-brain calcium imaging (Schrödel et al., 2013; Venkatachalam et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2016), identifying neurons across animals is additionally challenging because the nuclear localized markers that are used tend to obscure morphological features that would otherwise assist in neural identification.
evidence: Supported by citations to calcium imaging studies and reasoning about the technical challenge

claim: The fDNC model is based on the transformer network architecture.
source: We present an automated method to track and identify neurons in C. elegans, called 'fast Deep Neural Correspondence' or fDNC, based on the transformer network architecture.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract about the model architecture

claim: The fDNC model is trained once on empirically derived semi-synthetic data.
source: The model is trained once on empirically derived semi-synthetic data and then predicts neural correspondence across held-out real animals.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract about the training approach

claim: The same pre-trained fDNC model both tracks neurons across time and identifies corresponding neurons across individuals.
source: The same pre-trained model both tracks neurons across time and identifies corresponding neurons across individuals.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract about model capabilities

claim: Using only position information, the fDNC method achieves 79.1% accuracy at tracking neurons within an individual.
source: Using only position information, the method achieves 79.1% accuracy at tracking neurons within an individual and 64.1% accuracy at identifying neurons across individuals.
evidence: Quantitative performance metric reported in the abstract

claim: Using only position information, the fDNC method achieves 64.1% accuracy at identifying neurons across individuals.
source: Using only position information, the method achieves 79.1% accuracy at tracking neurons within an individual and 64.1% accuracy at identifying neurons across individuals.
evidence: Quantitative performance metric reported in the abstract

claim: The fDNC method achieves 78.2% accuracy at identifying neurons across individuals when applied to a dataset published by Chaudhary et al., 2021.
source: Accuracy at identifying neurons across individuals is even higher (78.2%) when the model is applied to a dataset published by another group (Chaudhary et al., 2021).
evidence: Quantitative performance metric reported in the abstract with citation

claim: The fDNC method achieves 74.7% accuracy when using color information from NeuroPAL.
source: Accuracy reaches 74.7% on our dataset when using color information from NeuroPAL.
evidence: Quantitative performance metric reported in the abstract

claim: fDNC does not require straightening or transforming the animal into a canonical coordinate system.
source: Unlike previous methods, fDNC does not require straightening or transforming the animal into a canonical coordinate system.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract about method advantages

claim: The fDNC method predicts correspondence in 10 ms.
source: The method is fast and predicts correspondence in 10 ms making it suitable for future real-time applications.
evidence: Quantitative timing measurement reported in the abstract

claim: The 10 ms prediction time makes fDNC suitable for future real-time applications.
source: The method is fast and predicts correspondence in 10 ms making it suitable for future real-time applications.
evidence: Inference based on the measured speed

claim: Tracking neurons within an individual across time is needed to extract calcium dynamics from neurons during freely moving population calcium imaging.

claim: Very fast real-time tracking will be needed to bring closed-loop techniques such as brain-machine interfaces and optical patch clamping to moving animals.

claim: Most automated methods for C. elegans focus on finding the extrinsic similarity between one neuron configuration and another.

evidence: Supported by citations to existing real-time methods

claim: To be used in a real-time closed loop application, the fDNC model would need to be combined with faster segmentation algorithms because current segmentation algorithms are too slow for real-time use.
source: We note that to be used in a real-time closed loop application, our fDNC model would need to be combined with faster segmentation algorithms because current segmentation algorithms are too slow for real-time use.
evidence: Authors' assessment of system requirements

claim: Because segmentation can be easily parallelized, faster segmentation algorithms are expected to be developed soon.
source: Because segmentation can be easily paralellized, we expect that faster segmentation algorithms will be developed soon.
evidence: Authors' expectation about future developments

claim: Many advantages of the fDNC model stem from its use of the transformer architecture in combination with supervised learning.
source: Many of the advantages listed here stem from the fDNC model's use of the transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) in combination with supervised learning.
evidence: Authors' summary of methodological advantages with citation

claim: By using supervised learning on empirically derived semi-synthetic training data of animals in a variety of different poses and orientations, the model is forced to learn relative spatial features that are informative for finding neural correspondence.
source: By using supervised learning on empirically derived semi-synthetic training data of animals in a variety of different poses and orientations, the model is forced to learn relative spatial features within the neurons that are informative for finding neural correspondence across many postures and conditions.
evidence: Authors' explanation of how the training approach works

claim: The transformer architecture leverages recent advances in GPU parallel processing for speed and efficiency.
source: Finally, the transformer architecture leverages recent advances in GPU parallel processing for speed and efficiency, which is an important step toward future real-time applications.
evidence: Description of computational advantages

claim: The simulator transforms neural positions of a real worm and introduces noise to generate new semi-synthetic individuals.
source: The simulator transforms the neural positions of a real worm and introduces noise to generate new semi-synthetic individuals.
evidence: Description shown in Figure 1B

claim: The fDNC model uses a multi-head attention mechanism to compute features.
source: The features are computed via a multi-head attention mechanism.
evidence: Description of architecture shown in Figure 1F

claim: The simulator starts by straightening the worm in the XY plane using its centerline so that it lies in a canonical worm coordinate system.
source: The simulator starts by straightening the worm in the XY plane using its centerline so that it now lies in a canonical worm coordinate system.
evidence: Description of simulator operation

claim: To introduce animal-to-animal variability in relative neural position, a non-rigid transformation is applied to the neuron point cloud using coherent point drift (CPD).
source: To introduce animal-to-animal variability in relative neural position, a non-rigid transformation is applied to the neuron point cloud against a template randomly selected from recordings of the real observed worms using coherent point drift (CPD) (Myronenko and Song, 2010).
evidence: Description of simulator operation with citation

claim: To simulate missing neurons and segmentation errors, spurious neurons are randomly added and some true neurons are randomly removed for up to 20% of the observed neurons.
source: To simulate missing neurons and segmentation errors, spurious neurons are randomly added, and some true neurons are randomly removed, for up to 20% of the observed neurons.
evidence: Description of simulator operation

claim: The simulator randomly rescales the animal's size by up to 5%.
source: Lastly, to account for variability in animals' size and orientation, a random affine transformation in the XY plane is applied that rescaled the animal's size by up to 5%.
evidence: Description of simulator operation

claim: Centerlines generated by the simulator were directly sampled from recordings of real individuals.
source: Centerlines generated by the simulator were directly sampled from recordings of real individuals.
evidence: Description of simulator data source

claim: The magnitude of added Gaussian noise in the simulator was set to have a standard deviation of 0.42 µm.
source: The magnitude of added Gaussian noise was arbitrarily set to have a standard deviation of 0.42 µm.
evidence: Quantitative parameter specification

claim: The fDNC model is implemented in the automatic differentiation framework PyTorch.
source: The deep neural correspondence model (fDNC) is an artificial neural network based on the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) architecture (Figure 1C) and is implemented in the automatic differentiation framework PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2017).
evidence: Description of implementation with citations

claim: For each worm, approximately 120 neurons are segmented and passed to the fDNC model.
source: For each worm, approximately 120 neurons are segmented and passed to the fDNC model.
evidence: Description of typical input size

claim: The input neuron sequences are randomly shuffled for both template worm and test worm to eliminate the possibility that information from the original sequence order is used.
source: The input neuron sequences are randomly shuffled for both template worm and test worm. This eliminates the possibility that the information from the original sequence order is used.
evidence: Description of preprocessing step and its purpose

claim: Each layer of the fDNC model consists of two sub-layers: a multi-head self-attention mechanism and a fully connected feed-forward network.
source: Each layer consists of two sub-layers: a multi-head self-attention mechanism (Vaswani et al., 2017) and a fully connected feed-forward network.
evidence: Description of model architecture with citation

claim: The fDNC implementation sets the number of heads in the multi-head attention module to be eight.
source: In our implementation, we set the number of heads in the multi-head attention module to be eight and we set the dimension of our feature vectors to be 128.
evidence: Description of hyperparameter choice

claim: The fDNC implementation sets the dimension of feature vectors to be 128.
source: In our implementation, we set the number of heads in the multi-head attention module to be eight and we set the dimension of our feature vectors to be 128.
evidence: Description of hyperparameter choice

claim: The best set of hyperparameters was chosen by evaluating on a validation set distinct from the training set and from any data used for evaluation.
source: We chose the best set of the hyperparameters (details in Training section) by evaluating on a validation set, which is distinct from the training set and also from any data used for evaluation.
evidence: Description of hyperparameter selection procedure

claim: A residual connection and layer normalization are employed for each sub-layer in the fDNC model.
source: A residual connection (He et al., 2016) and layer normalization (Jl et al., 2016) are employed for each sub-layer, as is widely used in artificial neural networks.
evidence: Description of architectural components with citations

claim: The fDNC model finds the most probable correspondence by solving a maximum weight bipartite matching problem using the Hungarian algorithm.
source: We also find the most probable correspondence between the two sets of neurons by solving a maximum weight bipartite matching problem where the weights are given by the inner products between test and template worm embeddings. This is a classic combinatorial optimization problem, and it can be solved in polynomial time using the Hungarian algorithm (Kuhn, 1955).
evidence: Description of optimization procedure with citation

claim: The fDNC model was trained for 12 hr on a 2.40 GHz Intel machine with NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPU.
source: The model was trained for 12 hr on a 2.40 GHz Intel machine with NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPU.
evidence: Description of training procedure

claim: A cross-entropy loss function was used to train the fDNC model.
source: We performed supervised learning with ground truth matches provided by the semi-synthetically generated data. A cross-entropy loss function was used.
evidence: Description of training procedure

claim: All the fDNC models trained converged after 12 hr of training.
source: All the models converged after 12 hr of training.
evidence: Observation from training

claim: The model with 6 layers and 128 dimensional embedding space was chosen because it reaches the highest performance.
source: We chose the model with 6 layers and 128 dimensional embedding space since it reaches the highest performance and increasing the complexity of the model did not appear to increase the performance dramatically.
evidence: Explanation of model selection based on validation results

claim: Increasing the complexity of the model beyond 6 layers and 128 dimensions did not appear to increase the performance dramatically.
source: We chose the model with 6 layers and 128 dimensional embedding space since it reaches the highest performance and increasing the complexity of the model did not appear to increase the performance dramatically.
evidence: Observation from hyperparameter search

claim: In the evaluation, every segmented neuron in the test or template (whichever has fewer) is assigned a match.
source: Every segmented neuron in the test or template (whichever has fewer) is assigned a match.
evidence: Description of evaluation procedure

claim: Accuracy is defined as the number of proposed matches that agree with ground truth, divided by the total number of ground truth matches.
source: Accuracy is defined as the number of proposed matches that agree with ground truth, divided by the total number of ground truth matches.
evidence: Definition of evaluation metric

claim: CPD is used to find the optimal non-rigid transformation to align the test worm with respect to the template worm.
source: In our implementation, CPD is used to find the optimal non-rigid transformation to align the test worm with respect to the template worm.
evidence: Description of baseline method implementation

claim: The color matching model measures similarity of color for each pair of neurons as the inverse of the Kullback–Leibler divergence between their normalized color features.
source: Then the similarity of color for each pair of neurons is measured as the inverse of the Kullback–Leibler divergence between their normalized color features.
evidence: Description of color model

claim: To calculate the final combined matching matrix, the color similarity matrix is added to the position matching log probability matrix from the fDNC model.
source: To calculate the final combined matching matrix, we add the color similarity matrix to the position matching log probability matrix from our fDNC model.
evidence: Description of how color and position information are combined

claim: The matching results are not particularly sensitive to the choice of λ.
source: We note the matching results are not particularly sensitive to the choice of λ.
evidence: Observation about parameter sensitivity

source: In particular, each layer of the neural network contains thousands of artificial neurons performing the same computation.

source: Computations for each neuron in a layer can all be performed in parallel and modern GPUs have as many as 3500 CUDA cores.

source: Labeling one volume has no dependencies on any previous volumes and therefore each volume can be processed simultaneously.
